justification: The article delivers on its stated angle: every surprising claim (emoji Length==2, the char/Rune/text-element gap, the Turkish-I flip) is run live through the site's harness with real output, not just asserted, and that is a genuine differentiator against the Microsoft Learn pages it competes with, which explain these facts in prose with illustrative-only snippets. The ordinal-vs-culture material is precise and the worked example (a `--silent` flag matcher under `tr-TR`) is original — it does not reuse best-practices-strings.md's own canonical 'Bill'/'BILL' example, which I fetched and compared directly. The StringBuilder-vs-naive-concatenation section handles the rounds-to-zero timing exactly as instructed: it reports the byte-allocation numbers precisely (400,519,976 B vs 49,248 B, an 8,100x ratio it does state, which the code's measured allocation bytes genuinely support) but explicitly declines to quantify the wall-clock ratio, saying only that StringBuilder 'finish[ed] too fast for Stopwatch at this size to tell apart from zero' and that time 'moved in the same direction' — qualitative, not fabricated, exactly per the writer's stated approach. No filler intro or boilerplate conclusion: the opening sentence states a concrete surprising fact and the closing paragraph ties back into the piece's own earlier point rather than summarizing headings. Headings are all content-specific (no 'Introduction'/'Conclusion'/'Key Takeaways'), and a heading-by-heading comparison against generics.md, garbage-collection.md, async-await.md and value-types-vs-reference-types.md in this same pillar shows no templated repetition. No placeholder or NEEDS_MARKUS markers, no ad code. Front matter title and description are accurate and non-clickbait. I spot-checked the seven distinctive quoted/attributed passages against the live cited pages: the immutability paraphrase, the StringInfo 'text element' definition ('a base character, a surrogate pair, or a combining character sequence'), the pre-.NET-5 StringInfo bug note, the Substring/Span cost claim ('creates a new string to hold the substring'), and the best-practices-strings Ordinal/OrdinalIgnoreCase default-recommendation summary all match their cited pages accurately (verbatim where quoted, faithfully paraphrased where not) and are not closely-paraphrased copying of the source's own sentence structure. One passage does not hold up: the sentence 'Because each `+=` "creates a new `String` object for each concatenation operation"' presents a phrase in quotation marks with no adjacent citation link, and I fetched the full StringBuilder Remarks/'StringBuilder versus String type' section verbatim — the actual sentence there is 'each operation that appears to modify a String object actually creates a new string,' and no sentence on that page (checked heading-by-heading) contains 'for each concatenation operation.' That is either a misremembered/fabricated quotation dressed in quotation marks or a genuine quote from an uncited source; either way it fails the binding 'cite where the claim is made, and make sure that page supports that clause' rule and touches the 'never fabricate' rule directly enough to hold the score below the 8.5 bar on its own. `node tools/run-code.mjs` was not re-run by this critic (technical editor's remit); this review is scoped to originality, filler and sourcing honesty per the AdSense rubric.
